passage: Wednesday. Yamini stopped me by the printer and asked if I had a minute to look at her budget sheet, because she said I was “the one who really knows formulas.” My first thought was, oh no, I have my own deadline. But she looked so hopeful and asked so politely that I said yes. Ten minutes later she'd fixed her own error with one hint from me and said, “Thank you, that was exactly what I needed.” I felt oddly warm and tall for the rest of the afternoon. I had assumed asking was a burden. It felt like being trusted. I'll offer next time before she has to ask. — Aadhya

qa.q: Where did Yamini stop Aadhya?
qa.a: Yamini stopped Aadhya by the printer.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel after helping Yamini?
qa.a: Aadhya felt warm and trusted, and proud enough to feel tall, after first having a flash of worry about a personal deadline.

qa.q: What did Aadhya learn about being asked?
qa.a: Aadhya learned that being asked felt like trust and not like a burden, and decided to offer help before Yamini has to ask.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel after asking for help?
qa.a: Yamini was hopeful and polite, and afterwards probably feels relieved and grateful, since she said the help was exactly what she needed.

grounding: A person approached for advice feels trusted and pleased rather than burdened.

passage: I'm Siddharth, and for years I thought people asking me for help was a burden. Then Dhruv, a junior from my team, stopped by my desk one evening. "Sorry to disturb you. Could I ask your advice on the vendor negotiation? You've done it before." He looked nervous, apologising twice. I was surprised by how good it felt. He had chosen me. We talked for fifteen minutes. I shared what had gone wrong in my first negotiation, and he took notes. Walking home, I kept smiling. The next morning he thanked me again, still sounding like he'd imposed. I told him, "Honestly, that was the best part of my week."

qa.q: What did Dhruv ask Siddharth's advice on?
qa.a: He asked for advice on the vendor negotiation.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling after helping Dhruv?
qa.a: Siddharth felt trusted and pleased, smiling on the walk home, surprised by how good it felt to be chosen.

qa.q: What could Dhruv take from Siddharth's reply the next morning?
qa.a: That asking at a suitable time often makes the other person feel valued, so there is no need to over-apologise.

qa.q: How does Dhruv seem to see his own request?
qa.a: Dhruv seems to see it as an imposition, looking nervous and apologising twice, overestimating the burden.

grounding: A worker describes being asked for advice and feeling trusted and pleased, while the asker worries about imposing.

passage:
Ward supervisor's note, Friday.
Jasleen, one of our new nurses, asked Akash today how he manages the handover notes so quickly. She apologised first, saying she knew he was busy. I watched Akash's face change. He had been tired all shift, but he straightened up, pulled out his own notebook and showed her his short system of symbols. He spent ten minutes with her during the quiet hour. Later he told me, "Nobody's asked me anything like that before. It felt good to be trusted." Jasleen still looked worried that she had troubled him. I will tell her that asking at a quiet moment, as she did, was exactly right.

qa.q: What did Jasleen ask Akash about?
qa.a: She asked how he manages the handover notes so quickly.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when Jasleen asked him?
qa.a: He felt trusted and pleased, straightening up despite being tired, glad that someone valued his system.

qa.q: What will the supervisor tell Jasleen, and why?
qa.a: That asking at a quiet moment was exactly right, so she need not worry about imposing.

qa.q: How does Jasleen see her request?
qa.a: Jasleen sees it as troubling a busy colleague, apologising first and still looking worried afterwards.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a colleague feeling trusted and pleased when asked for advice, while the asker worries about imposing.

passage:
Dear Diary, Wednesday
Tanuja from accounts messaged me today: "Could I take 20 minutes of your time? I'm preparing for my first client presentation and you did such a good one last month." She added "So sorry to bother you!" three times.
Honestly? It made my day. I've been feeling invisible at work lately, and here was someone who'd noticed. We met in the canteen at four. I went through my slides with her and told her the things I'd do differently. She kept thanking me like I'd done a huge favour.
Funny how she thinks she's imposing. It was the most useful I've felt in weeks. 😊
Rashmi

qa.q: How much time did Tanuja ask for?
qa.a: Tanuja asked for 20 minutes.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel about being asked?
qa.a: Rashmi felt valued and happy; it made the day after feeling invisible at work.

qa.q: What could Rashmi say to help Tanuja feel less worried?
qa.a: Rashmi could tell Tanuja that the request felt good, and that there's no need to apologise for asking at a reasonable time.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see her request?
qa.a: Tanuja sees it as a bother, apologising three times and thanking Rashmi as if for a huge favour.

grounding: A diary shows a worker feeling trusted and valued when asked for advice, while the asker overestimates the imposition.
